title: Tech Lead — Level 1: Foundations
description: The baseline of technical leadership: role definition, code review, estimation, and basic architecture vocabulary.

questions.prompt: "What does a tech lead actually do?" — give the crisp interview answer distinguishing the role from senior engineer and engineering manager.
questions.answer_notes: A tech lead owns the technical outcome of a team's work: architecture and technical direction, cross-cutting decisions and trade-offs, unblocking others, technical quality (reviews, standards), and translating between product goals and engineering reality. Unlike a senior engineer, individual output is secondary to multiplying the team's output. Unlike an EM, the lever is technical direction, not people management (careers, performance, hiring) — though the roles overlap and vary by company; saying you'd clarify the split in each org is a plus.
questions.difficulty_rationale: Opens nearly every tech-lead interview; the answer frames everything after it.

questions.prompt: What is the primary purpose of code review in a healthy team?
options: Sharing knowledge and catching design/correctness issues early — building shared ownership of the codebase
Proving who the strongest programmer on the team is
Ensuring every line follows the lead's personal style
Creating an audit trail to assign blame after incidents
questions.answer_notes: Reviews catch bugs and design drift cheaply, spread context so no code is single-owner, and teach conventions. A lead should also say what reviews are NOT for: style nitpicks belong to formatters/linters; reviews should be timely (a day, not a week), kind in tone, and proportionate to risk. Trust grows when review effort matches change risk.
questions.difficulty_rationale: Basic culture question testing whether the candidate sees reviews as collaboration.

questions.prompt: Product asks: "How long will this feature take?" Walk through how you produce and communicate an estimate you can stand behind.
questions.answer_notes: Decompose into tasks small enough to reason about; estimate ranges, not points in time; add explicit buffers for the unknowns you can name (integration, review, QA, deploy) and state assumptions. Communicate as a range with confidence ('2-3 weeks if the API behaves as documented; the risky part is X, we'll know more after a 1-day spike'). Update the estimate when facts change — early and loudly, never silently. Bonus: distinguish estimate (fact-based) from commitment (negotiated) and offer scope cuts as the lever, not quality.
questions.difficulty_rationale: Basic but revealing; interviewers listen for ranges, assumptions, and re-communication.

questions.prompt: A 6-person startup asks whether to start with microservices. What is the defensible default answer?
options: Start with a well-modularized monolith; split services later only when scaling or organizational pain justifies the operational cost
Always microservices — they are the modern standard
Let each developer choose their own architecture per feature
questions.answer_notes: Microservices buy independent deployment/scaling and team autonomy at the price of distributed-systems complexity: network failure modes, data consistency, observability, CI/CD multiplication. A 6-person team has no org-scaling problem to solve. The mature answer: modular monolith with clean internal boundaries (so future extraction is possible), split only on measured pain — a hot component needing independent scaling, or teams blocking each other.
questions.difficulty_rationale: Classic judgment check against resume-driven architecture.

questions.prompt: Explain technical debt to a non-technical stakeholder, including why some debt is fine and how you decide what to pay down.
questions.answer_notes: Analogy that lands: debt is borrowing speed now at an interest rate paid later — some loans are smart (shipping fast to validate a market), some are payday loans (skipping tests on core billing code). Not all debt is worth paying: prioritize by interest actually paid — code you touch weekly and that causes bugs/slowdowns gets paid down; ugly-but-stable corners don't. Concrete practice: track debt visibly, budget a steady percentage of capacity (not a mythical 'refactoring sprint someday'), and tie paydown items to the features they unblock so the business sees the return.
questions.difficulty_rationale: Basic stakeholder-communication staple for lead roles.

questions.prompt: What is the core reason CI/CD with small, frequent releases beats large scheduled releases?
options: Small changes make failures rare, cheap to diagnose, and fast to roll back — shrinking both risk and feedback time
It eliminates the need for testing
It lets managers see more releases on the dashboard
questions.answer_notes: Batch size drives risk: a 500-commit release makes any failure a needle-in-haystack; a 5-commit release localizes it. Frequent deploys keep the deploy machinery exercised, enable fast rollback, and shorten user feedback loops. Reference the DORA research linking deploy frequency + lead time with lower change-failure rate. Prerequisites to mention: automated test gates, feature flags to decouple deploy from release, rollback paths.
questions.difficulty_rationale: Basic delivery-culture knowledge every lead is expected to articulate.

questions.prompt: A teammate strongly disagrees with your technical decision. Walk through how you handle it (a behavioral staple — answer in STAR-ready form).
questions.answer_notes: Steps interviewers listen for: genuinely understand their position first (steelman it back to them); separate matters of taste from matters of consequence; look for data or a cheap experiment to decide (prototype, benchmark, time-boxed spike); if it remains judgment, decide explicitly, document the reasoning and revisit-triggers, and ask for disagree-and-commit — offering the same in return when they own decisions. Never: pull rank first, litigate in the group channel, or let it fester unresolved. Have a real story ready: situation, the disagreement, how it resolved, what you learned — including one where you turned out to be wrong.
questions.difficulty_rationale: Asked in almost every lead interview, usually behaviorally.

questions.prompt: Which 'definition of done' best reflects professional engineering standards for a user-facing feature?
options: Code reviewed and merged, covered by tests, observable in production (metrics/logs), documented where needed, and verified working in the real environment
The code compiles on the developer's machine
The developer says it works and the demo went fine
The PR is open and someone will look at it eventually
questions.answer_notes: Done means: shipped, verified, observable, and maintainable by others. Leads should institutionalize this as a checklist so 'done' isn't renegotiated per task. Mention that observability at launch (dashboards, alerts) is part of the feature, not an afterthought — you can't support what you can't see.
questions.difficulty_rationale: Basic quality-bar question; weak answers reveal demo-driven engineering.
